title: Logical gate set tomography
authors: Piper C. Wysocki, Juan Gonzalez De Mendoza, Karl Mayer, Natalie C. Brown, Ciaran Ryan-Anderson, Jalan A. Ziyad, Jordan H. Hines, Daniel G. Hothem, Corey I. Ostrove, Timothy J. Proctor, Kevin C. Young, Robin J. Blume-Kohout, Charles H. Baldwin, Kenneth M. Rudinger
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.
summary: This paper introduces Logical Gate Set Tomography (logical GST) to deeply characterize noise in quantum error correction codes. By applying this technique to trapped-ion hardware and simulators, the authors distinguish between simple stochastic errors and more complex coherent or non-Markovian errors. This work is crucial for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing by providing actionable diagnostics for hardware improvement.
main_problem: The goal is to thoroughly characterize noise in quantum error correction (QEC) by understanding the *form* of the noise (e.g., Markovian vs. non-Markovian, Pauli-stochastic vs. coherent), rather than just measuring effective noise rates.
main_result: The study found that while initial hardware data suggested Pauli-stochastic errors, detailed simulation revealed strong evidence for coherent logical errors and non-Markovianity, allowing for error attribution to specific physical sources.
method: The authors introduce and apply Logical Gate Set Tomography (logical GST), which extends standard GST to characterize effective operations acting only on the logical degrees of freedom.
model_or_system: The work uses the seven-qubit Steane code ($\llbracket 7, 1, 3 rbracket$) for logical encoding and is implemented on the Quantinuum System Model H1 (a 20-qubit trapped-ion processor), supplemented by a detailed system emulator (H1-1E).
key_observables: Gate fidelity, diamond distance, logical Pauli-stochastic error rates, logical non-Markovianity signatures, and coherent logical error parameters.
important_parameters: The analysis involves model selection using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and fitting parameters related to coherent error generators (FOGI parameters).
main_assumptions: The standard GST model often assumes the Markovian property (no context dependence), which the paper tests by analyzing syndrome correlations and comparing experimental vs. simulated results.
figures_summary: Figures schematically detail the logical GST protocol, show syndrome correlations across time steps, and illustrate the comparison between hardware measurements and emulator predictions regarding error types.
paper_structure: The paper introduces logical GST, details the protocol for characterizing the logical gate set, analyzes hardware data to identify error types (Pauli-stochastic), and contrasts these findings with detailed emulator simulations to pinpoint underlying physical error mechanisms like coherence and non-Markovianity.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of GST to the logical level provides a powerful diagnostic tool for fault-tolerant quantum computation, moving beyond simple fidelity metrics to diagnose the fundamental nature of noise (e.g., memory effects, coherence) in physical hardware.
